Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09

Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Patel (Redwood SE), Rita Gomez (Redwood SE), Jared Miller (Brightscale CTO), Priya Shah (Brightscale ML Eng), Omar Ruiz (Brightscale Infra)

Summary: Deep dive on throughput tuning across continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token_limit), and KV cache behaviour.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining um today we want to do a focused deep dive on throughput tuning for Brightscale, especially around continuous batching and scheduler knobs, we have Lucas and Rita from the SE side to go into the runtime details.
[00:12] Jared Miller: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. Our goal is to get predictable token throughput at p95 latency under 200 ms for the chat use-case, and keep costs under our SLO.
[00:23] Lucas Patel: Cool. Before we dig in, can you remind us of your typical request distribution? tokens per request, concurrency?
[00:30] Priya Shah: Sure, so median prompt is about 120 tokens, 95th is around 700 when customers send context, but most are 150-250. Staging concurrency today is ~120 qps, but peak bursts hit 400 qps for few minutes.
[00:48] Lucas Patel: That helps. Two big levers we'll focus on: continuous batching behavior (how the runtime aggregates inflight requests) and scheduler knobs - things like max_num_seqs, token_limit_per_batch, and queueing latency caps.
[01:05] Omar Ruiz: Quick Q - we 're running on our VPC with on-prem GPUs (DGX-like). Network is fine, but we're worried about NUMA and PCIe affecting throughput with big batches.
[01:16] Rita Gomez: Right, NUMA/pCIe swaps (sic) can show up as tail latency; when you increase batch size you sometimes push into multi-GPU or across NUMA boundaries, which gives non-linear runtime costs. We usually recommend measuring p99 when changing max_num_seqs.
[01:31] Priya Shah: On that note, what do you mean exactly by max_num_seqs?
[01:34] Lucas Patel: max_num_seqs is the scheduler cap on how many sequences the runtime will pack into a single batched kernel call. For example, with 8k context and 7B model, you might set max_num_seqs to 32 or 64 depending on memory headroom; it's a tradeoff - higher means more throughput but higher tail latency and memory pressure.
[01:51] Jared Miller: Is there a rule of thumb to pick it?
[01:53] Lucas Patel: Start with an estimate: target batch size = (GPU_mem_for_batch) / (avg_seq_mem). Practically, we ship sample configs: for 7B on A100-40GB we'd start with max_num_seqs=32 and token_limit ~1024 for chat workloads. For 13B you'd start lower, maybe 16. But we have knobs to force earlier flushes based on queue wait time.
[02:12] Maya Chen: Also continuous batching parameters - you can configure target batch latency (how long the scheduler will wait to try to fill a batch) and queue-time caps, so you can balance throughput vs p95 latency.
[02:23] Omar Ruiz: How does KV cache interaction work with batching? We saw our KV cache hit-rate drop when we upped batching during a PoC.
[02:31] Lucas Patel: Good observation. If requests share prefixes or reuse context, KV cache hits reduce compute. But if you shuffle requests aggressively, you may lose locality. The runtime uses per-session KV cache keyed by conversation id; batching doesn't evict the cache but the effective hit-rate depends on request routing. For continuous batching we recommend enabling prefix-aware scheduling if your workload has many repeated system prompts.
[02:56] Priya Shah: We do have repeated system prompts for onboarding flows. How do you enable prefix-aware scheduling?
[03:02] Rita Gomez: It's a scheduling mode - you tag requests with a hint (conversation_id or trace) and the scheduler will try to group ones with shared prefix in the same batch. Tradeoff is slightly increased queueing to get those matches.
[03:15] Jared Miller: About token limits - what's the effect of token_limit on throughput?
[03:19] Lucas Patel: token_limit controls max tokens processed per request inside a batch step. If you set too high, you increase average per-step compute. Setting token_limit to something close to your 95th percentile reduces wasted compute in rare huge requests. We also have dynamic step-splitting: long requests can be chunked across multiple kernel calls; this reduces max latency but may slightly increase total GPU cycles due to kernel overhead.
[03:44] Priya Shah: We saw in preliminary runs that when we constrain token_limit to 512 the throughput increased but p50 latency improved much more than p95.
[03:52] Lucas Patel: Expected. p95 is driven by long tails - long prompts or cross-NUMA effects. For p95 focus on queue caps and max_num_seqs; for average throughput reduce token_limit and tune batch latency.
[04:05] Omar Ruiz: Can you run through an example config for a 7B quantized model on our DGX?
[04:10] Lucas Patel: Sure. Example (starting point): max_num_seqs=32, target_batch_latency_ms=8, queue_max_wait_ms=20, token_limit=1024, prefix_aware=true, continuous_batching=true. For 4-bit quantized 7B models memory headroom is higher so you can push max_num_seqs up a bit.
[04:30] Jared Miller: You mentioned quantization - any quality or perf gotchas for 4-bit vs 8-bit?
[04:35] Rita Gomez: 4-bit quant gets you better memory/cost and often higher throughput because you can increase packing. Quality varies by model/quant method - some open models degrade slightly on certain tasks. We recommend evals on your prompt set. Also for 4-bit sometimes kernel paths change and latency characteristics differ; measure both p50 and p95.
[04:55] Priya Shah: Is there support for mixed-precision or hybrid quant?
[04:58] Lucas Patel: Yes, you can do per-layer exceptions - Redwood Optimize can recommend layers to keep in higher precision if you see quality regressions. That is more of a model-ops step but supported in private/dedicated flows.
[05:10] Maya Chen: Another runtime knob: scheduler backpressure thresholds. If queue grows beyond X, the runtime can start shedding lower-priority requests or route to a cheaper model variant - do you use that?
[05:20] Jared Miller: We prefer failing fast rather than big latency spikes; shedding low-priority background requests sounds good.
[05:25] Lucas Patel: We typically set two thresholds: soft_limit (start routing to fallback variant or throttle) and hard_limit (reject or return 429). For multi-tenant on-prem you can also reserve slots per route.
[05:36] Omar Ruiz: Network/PCIe - if we see non-linear slowdowns at larger batch sizes, is NUMA binding a typical cause?
[05:42] Rita Gomez: Yes. On machines with multiple sockets, you can end up crossing NUMA domains if tensors get split across GPUs or if host memory copies are needed. Pinning processes and using correct CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES ordering helps; also check NVLink topology and ensure batches fit per-GPU memory.
[06:00] Priya Shah: Any specific metrics we should capture during our 48-hour run?
[06:04] Lucas Patel: Capture per-request latency histograms, batch sizes distribution, KV cache hit-rate, GPU utilization, GPU memory headroom, kernel occupancy, and queue wait times. Also log trace IDs to correlate long tail requests with specific prompt sizes or origins.
[06:18] Maya Chen: We'll share a benchmark spreadsheet template. That normally includes sample dashboards and queries to extract p50/p95/p99 and batch-size heatmaps.
[06:26] Jared Miller: Great. A quick question on continuous batching - does it interact badly with stateful sessions (chat) where you need to maintain KV caches per session?
[06:34] Lucas Patel: Not badly - the runtime maintains per-session KV cache. The caveat is you must preserve session ids in requests. If you use prefix_aware scheduling it'll try to batch same sessions together; otherwise, KV cache benefits come from request hitting the same session on the same worker. For multi-worker routing ensure sticky routing or shared cache (but shared cache is more complicated for on-prem).
[06:55] Omar Ruiz: For our VPC private deployment, anything special about encryption/KMS that affects perf?
[07:00] Rita Gomez: KMS calls for key unwrap happen primarily at model load time; in steady-state inference there is minimal per-request KMS overhead provided keys are cached locally in HSM/KMS-integrated agent. Network encryption adds negligible CPU cost compared to large token compute on GPU.
[07:14] Priya Shah: We run some pods that move models between nodes at scale. Do you recommend model pinning for throughput runs?
[07:20] Lucas Patel: For consistent benchmarking yes - pin the model to the node(s) so you remove model movement variance. In production you can use autoscaling but that will add variance.
[07:30] Jared Miller: What about warmup? Should we pre-warm KV cache?
[07:33] Lucas Patel: Definitely. Pre-warm with representative traffic or a targeted prefix replay. Warm KV cache reduces first-window latency and can significantly improve p95 in early bursts.
[07:43] Priya Shah: We're concerned about cost. Is there a recommended sweet spot for batch sizes to maximize tokens/sec / dollar?
[07:49] Lucas Patel: There's usually a convex curve: small batches underutilize the GPU; very large batches deliver marginal throughput gains but increase tail latency and may force higher memory instance types. We often plot tokens/sec per GPU-hour across batch sizes to pick an economic optimum. Redwood Optimize can run that analysis for you if you provide sample traces.
[08:09] Rita Gomez: One pragmatic tip - enable adaptive batching that grows when queue is healthy but enforces strict queue_max_wait_ms to protect latency SLOs.
[08:18] Jared Miller: If we enable adaptive batching and prefix-aware scheduling, do we risk starvation for infrequent sessions?
[08:24] Lucas Patel: We mitigate that with fairness policies - reserve a fraction of batch capacity or a slot-based latency cap. Also lower-priority jobs can be routed to a cheaper model variant.
[08:34] Maya Chen: Ok we'll drop the config examples and a recommended benchmarking template in the follow-up email.
[08:40] Priya Shah: One practical debugging question - when we saw throughput drop in our tests, logs showed a lot of small kernel calls. What should we look for?
[08:47] Lucas Patel: That usually means either token_limit is too small causing many step calls, or queue flush policy is too aggressive, or there is fragmentation of sequences (different seq_lens) causing smaller effective kernel sizes. Check batch-size distribution and kernel invocation counts.
[09:05] Omar Ruiz: For observability, do you expose per-kernel timings?
[09:08] Rita Gomez: Yes, runtime can emit per-kernel micrometrics, batch composition metadata, and scheduling traces. We'll include the logging configuration we'll recommend.
[09:18] Jared Miller: Security/compliance note - we need audit logs for model loads and config changes. Is that available?
[09:22] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private includes audit logs and role-based access controls; we can share the SOC2 docs.
[09:28] Priya Shah: Last quick thing - any gotchas with mixed-precision and fused kernels on our setup?
[09:33] Lucas Patel: Fused kernels can give great throughput but are sensitive to tensor shapes; if your sequence length distribution is wide you may see less benefit. Mixed-precision rounding can also affect deterministic outputs. Recommend running the quantized/fused kernel path on a subset of prompts first.
[09:50] Maya Chen: Ok I think that's a good place to wrap. Recap: Redwood will send scheduler knobs doc, sample configs for 7B/13B quant settings, and a benchmark template. Brightscale will run the 48-hour throughput test and share request distribution and traces. We'll meet again to review results.
[10:07] Jared Miller: Sounds good - thanks everyone.
[10:10] Priya Shah: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
